questions.stem: A 47 year old man started isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide for tuberculosis 6 weeks ago. He now has 5 days of jaundice and vomiting, and today is disorientated in time. He has no history of liver disease. His ALT is 2900 IU/L (10–50), ALP 190 IU/L (25–115), bilirubin 160 μmol/L (<17) and INR 2.6.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Drug-induced liver injury has caused rapid loss of liver function in a previously normal liver: INR over 1.5 plus encephalopathy is acute liver failure.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Hepatotoxic drugs, encephalopathy, INR over 1.5, a huge ALT with a smaller ALP rise, and no prior liver disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute liver failure.

elim: Needs heavy drinking, with AST:ALT over 1.5 and an ALT rarely above 300.
Would give an ALP-dominant picture with dilated ducts.
Needs pre-existing cirrhosis; he has none.
Confusion with ataxia and eye signs, without an INR of 2.6.

steps.x: **A. Acute liver failure.** Encephalopathy + INR >1.5 in a previously healthy liver = acute liver failure; drugs are a key cause.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man who has drunk 70 units of alcohol a week for 25 years has 3 months of increasing abdominal swelling and tiredness. He has spider naevi on his chest, gynaecomastia, a palpable spleen and shifting dullness. His albumin is 27 g/L (35–50), platelets 76 × 10⁹/L (150–400) and INR 1.6.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Chronic liver failure from alcohol-related cirrhosis
questions.e: Gradual decline on a background of heavy drinking with stigmata of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension is chronic liver failure from cirrhosis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: 70 units of alcohol a week for 25 years
steps.x: Long-term alcohol, gradual course, stigmata of chronic liver disease, splenomegaly and low platelets from portal hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic liver failure from alcohol-related cirrhosis.

elim: Develops over days in a previously normal liver.
Gives acute pain and tender hepatomegaly, not spider naevi and gynaecomastia.
Raised JVP and no spider naevi or splenomegaly.
Low albumin and oedema, but no stigmata of liver disease or raised INR.

steps.x: **C. Chronic liver failure from alcohol-related cirrhosis.** Gradual decline + stigmata + portal hypertension = chronic liver failure on cirrhosis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman is admitted with acute liver failure after acute hepatitis A. She is drowsy and disorientated in time but obeys commands. Her INR is 2.4 and ALT 3800 IU/L (10–50). Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. She holds her arms out with wrists extended and fingers spread.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding?
o: Coarse, irregular flapping of the hands
Fine tremor at rest that improves on movement
Symmetrical sustained clonus at the wrists
questions.e: Asterixis, a coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, is a sign of grade II/III hepatic encephalopathy and a cardinal feature of liver failure.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Liver failure with encephalopathy; the arms held out to look for a flap.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coarse, irregular flapping of the hands.

elim: That describes a physiological or anxiety tremor.
Cerebellar sign.
Parkinson's disease.
Upper motor neurone or serotonin syndrome sign.

steps.x: **A. Coarse, irregular flapping of the hands.** Liver failure + encephalopathy = asterixis (hepatic flap).

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has compensated alcohol-related cirrhosis and has been stable for 2 years. Over 3 days she develops a productive cough, fever, jaundice and confusion. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her bilirubin has risen from 30 to 180 μmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute insult (here pneumonia) in someone with pre-existing cirrhosis causes rapid decompensation: acute-on-chronic liver failure.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Stable cirrhosis, then an infection, then sudden jaundice and encephalopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute-on-chronic liver failure.

elim: Occurs in pregnancy or with simple steatosis, not with a chest infection on cirrhosis.
No autoimmune features; there is a clear infective trigger.
Gives pain, ascites and tender hepatomegaly from venous obstruction.
Primary acute liver failure needs a previously normal liver.

steps.x: **B. Acute-on-chronic liver failure.** Cirrhosis + acute insult (infection, bleed, binge) = acute-on-chronic liver failure.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has type 2 diabetes, arthritis in his second and third knuckles and grey-bronze skin. He drinks 6 units of alcohol a week. He is admitted with new ascites, jaundice and confusion. His ferritin is 2800 μg/L (30–400) and transferrin saturation 88% (20–50). Hepatitis B and C serology are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his liver failure?
questions.e: Diabetes, MCP arthropathy, bronze skin and very high ferritin and transferrin saturation point to hereditary haemochromatosis, a cause of acute-on-chronic liver failure.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Classic iron-overload triad with high transferrin saturation and new decompensation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hereditary haemochromatosis.

elim: 6 units a week is too little.
Gives emphysema and low alpha-1 antitrypsin, not high iron.
No overdose history, and it would not explain the skin, joints and iron.
Presents young with neuropsychiatric signs and low caeruloplasmin.

steps.x: **C. Hereditary haemochromatosis.** Diabetes + bronze skin + MCP arthropathy + high transferrin saturation = haemochromatosis.

questions.stem: A 21 year old student with depression is brought in by her flatmate 3 days after a break-up. Since then she has vomited and has pain under her right ribs. She is jaundiced, with a tender liver edge and a coarse flapping tremor. Her ALT is 8400 IU/L (10–50) and INR 4.1.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause?
questions.e: The hepatic phase of paracetamol overdose (about day 3) gives vomiting, RUQ pain, a tender liver edge and features of liver failure such as asterixis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Possible deliberate overdose 3 days ago, then RUQ pain, a tender liver and asterixis with a massive ALT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Paracetamol overdose.

elim: Fever and Murphy's sign with only a modest ALT rise.
Possible, but the timeline after a crisis and the ALT over 8000 point to paracetamol.
Would cause hyperthermia and collapse at the time, not 3 days later.
Unconjugated jaundice with a normal ALT and INR.

steps.x: **E. Paracetamol overdose.** Day 3 after a possible overdose with RUQ pain and liver failure = paracetamol hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man drinks a bottle of vodka a day and binged heavily last weekend. He has 1 week of jaundice, anorexia and malaise. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. He has tender hepatomegaly. Blood tests have been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of results?
o: ALP-dominant rise with dilated bile ducts
ALT above 5000 IU/L with normal bilirubin
Normal liver enzymes with low platelets
questions.e: Alcoholic hepatitis gives a raised bilirubin, an AST:ALT ratio above 1.5 and a neutrophilia.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Chronic heavy drinking with a binge trigger, jaundice, low fever and tender liver: alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: AST:ALT ratio above 1.5 with neutrophilia.

elim: Obstructive pattern from stones or a tumour.
Paracetamol or viral pattern; alcohol rarely pushes ALT that high, and he is jaundiced.
Gilbert's or haemolysis.
He is jaundiced, so bilirubin must be raised.

steps.x: **C. AST:ALT ratio above 1.5 with neutrophilia.** Alcoholic hepatitis labs: high bilirubin, AST:ALT >1.5, neutrophilia.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman who drinks 90 units of alcohol a week has 10 days of jaundice and vomiting after a family wedding. She is now drowsy and has a flapping tremor and shifting dullness. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a large echobright liver and normal bile ducts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic heavy drinking with a binge, acute jaundice and fever, and in severe cases encephalopathy and ascites, is severe alcoholic hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: drowsy and has a flapping tremor
steps.x: Heavy drinker, binge trigger, jaundice with fever, plus encephalopathy and ascites (severe features).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severe alcoholic hepatitis.

elim: Needs biliary obstruction; the bile ducts are normal.
Epigastric pain to the back; would not give flap and ascites.
Would show a mass on ultrasound and develop slowly.
Confusion without jaundice, flap or ascites.

steps.x: **D. Severe alcoholic hepatitis.** Binge on heavy drinking + jaundice + fever ± encephalopathy/ascites = alcoholic hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis and ascites has 3 days of vague abdominal discomfort and increasing confusion. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and mildly tender, without guarding. Diagnostic paracentesis is done.
questions.q: Which complication has most likely occurred?
questions.e: In cirrhosis with ascites, fever, mild abdominal pain and new confusion with ascitic neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³ is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Cirrhotic with ascites, low-grade fever, mild tenderness, encephalopathy, ascitic neutrophilia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

elim: Would give peritonism and polymicrobial ascites with free air.
Gives weight loss and a rising AFP, not neutrophilic ascites.
Rising creatinine and oliguria; ascites is not infected.
Pain and worsening ascites but no ascitic neutrophilia.

steps.x: **E. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.** Cirrhosis + ascites + fever/confusion + ascitic neutrophils >250 = SBP.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with polycythaemia vera has 1 week of right upper quadrant pain and abdominal swelling. She has a tender liver edge 5 cm below the costal margin and shifting dullness. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. Her haemoglobin is 182 g/L (115–165). The site of her pain is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Right upper quadrant pain with a tender, enlarged liver.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A prothrombotic state with the triad of abdominal pain, ascites and tender hepatomegaly is Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis).

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: right upper quadrant pain and abdominal swelling
steps.x: Prothrombotic disease with pain, ascites and tender hepatomegaly: the Budd-Chiari triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Budd-Chiari syndrome.

elim: Fever and Murphy's sign, without ascites.
Jaundice and very high ALT, rarely rapid ascites.
No alcohol history.
Raised JVP and peripheral oedema would be present.

steps.x: **D. Budd-Chiari syndrome.** Pain + ascites + tender hepatomegaly in a prothrombotic patient = Budd-Chiari.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman at 34 weeks of her first pregnancy has 5 days of upper abdominal pain and generalised itch. Today she is jaundiced and vomiting. Her BP is 126/78 mmHg and pulse rate 104 bpm. Urine dipstick shows no protein. Her ALT is 520 IU/L (10–50), glucose 2.9 mmol/L and INR 1.9.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Third-trimester jaundice following abdominal pain and itch, with hypoglycaemia and a raised INR, is acute liver failure from acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: upper abdominal pain and generalised itch
steps.x: Late pregnancy, pain and itch then jaundice, with liver failure features (low glucose, high INR).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

elim: Hypertension and proteinuria with haemolysis; BP and urine are normal.
Possible, but needs travel or water exposure and would not explain this pattern without it.
Occurs in the first trimester without liver failure.
Itch and raised bile acids, without jaundice-led liver failure, hypoglycaemia or coagulopathy.

steps.x: **A. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy.** Third trimester + pain and itch → jaundice + low glucose + high INR = AFLP.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man who moved from China 20 years ago has cirrhosis with ascites and splenomegaly. He has never drunk alcohol and has a BMI of 23. He had a blood transfusion as a child. His ferritin and caeruloplasmin are normal. Hepatitis B surface antigen is positive and hepatitis B core IgG antibody positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his chronic liver failure?
questions.e: Viral hepatitis B is a major cause of chronic liver failure; a positive surface antigen with core IgG indicates chronic infection, often acquired at birth in endemic areas.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
From an endemic region, no alcohol, normal metabolic screen, HBsAg positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic hepatitis B infection.

elim: Usually a woman with raised IgG and ASMA.
Excluded by a normal ferritin.
Unlikely with a normal BMI.
Excluded by a normal caeruloplasmin.

steps.x: **B. Chronic hepatitis B infection.** Chronic HBsAg positivity is a key viral cause of cirrhosis and chronic liver failure.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has 8 days of jaundice and vomiting after eating shellfish in Egypt. Today he is confused. He is jaundiced with a tender, smooth liver edge. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. He has no stigmata of chronic liver disease.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Viral hepatitis has progressed to acute liver failure: encephalopathy and INR above 1.5 with a huge transaminase rise and a smaller rise in bilirubin and ALP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: no stigmata of chronic liver disease
steps.x: Acute hepatitis now with encephalopathy and an INR over 1.5 in a previously normal liver.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute liver failure.

elim: Needs biliary obstruction, with an ALP-dominant rise.
He has no background cirrhosis or stigmata.
Mild unconjugated jaundice; ALT and INR are normal.
Confusion and INR over 1.5 mean it is no longer uncomplicated.

steps.x: **B. Acute liver failure.** Encephalopathy + INR >1.5 + no prior liver disease = acute liver failure.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman is admitted 4 days after a paracetamol overdose. She is drowsy and has a hepatic flap. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg. The admitting doctor predicts her liver tests before the results return.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of results?
o: ALP markedly raised, with a normal ALT
ALT and ALP normal, with a low albumin only
ALT markedly raised, with a more modest rise in ALP and bilirubin
ALT normal, with a raised unconjugated bilirubin only
INR normal, with a raised gamma-GT
questions.e: Acute liver failure gives markedly raised transaminases with a more modest rise in ALP and bilirubin, and an INR above 1.5.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: drowsy and has a hepatic flap
steps.x: Paracetamol acute liver failure: hepatocyte necrosis dominates.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ALT markedly raised, with a more modest rise in ALP and bilirubin.

elim: That is cholestasis or obstruction.
Chronic malnutrition or nephrotic picture, not acute necrosis.
Haemolysis or Gilbert's.
Encephalopathy here implies the INR is raised.

steps.x: **C. ALT markedly raised, with a more modest rise in ALP and bilirubin.** Acute liver failure: huge ALT, modest ALP/bilirubin rise, INR >1.5.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has alcohol-related cirrhosis. His platelets are 64 × 10⁹/L (150–400). An endoscopy last year showed oesophageal varices. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. The registrar asks you to examine his abdomen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal examination?
questions.e: Portal hypertension in chronic liver failure causes splenomegaly (with low platelets from hypersplenism) and varices.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Cirrhosis with varices and low platelets: portal hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Splenomegaly.

elim: Polycystic kidney disease.
Gastric or pancreatic cancer.
Abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Gastric outlet or bowel obstruction.

steps.x: **D. Splenomegaly.** Portal hypertension = splenomegaly + varices + low platelets.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis has been stable on lactulose. She presents with confusion and black, tarry stools for 2 days. She has asterixis. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. Her haemoglobin is 74 g/L (115–165) and urea 18.2 mmol/L (2.5–7.8).
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of her encephalopathy?
questions.e: A GI bleed is an acute insult that decompensates cirrhosis: the blood protein load raises ammonia, triggering encephalopathy.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Melaena, low haemoglobin and a high urea (digested blood) in a cirrhotic with new encephalopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Upper gastrointestinal bleed.

elim: Gives tremor and agitation, but the melaena and anaemia point to a bleed.
Can cause confusion but would not explain melaena and a high urea.
Needs fever and abdominal tenderness; the bleed is clear here.
Would cause focal signs, not asterixis.

steps.x: **E. Upper gastrointestinal bleed.** Melaena + high urea + encephalopathy in cirrhosis = upper GI bleed precipitant.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with cirrhosis had a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placed 2 weeks ago for refractory ascites. His ascites has improved. His wife says he is now sleepy in the day and muddled. He has asterixis. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: TIPS diverts portal blood, rich in ammonia, past the liver, so the main complication is hepatic encephalopathy.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: sleepy in the day and muddled
steps.x: New confusion and asterixis soon after TIPS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatic encephalopathy.

elim: Rising creatinine and oliguria; TIPS tends to improve it.
Would give focal neurology, not asterixis.
Needs fever and tender abdomen; afebrile here.
TIPS lowers portal pressure, so bleeding is less likely, and he is stable.

steps.x: **A. Hepatic encephalopathy.** Main TIPS complication = hepatic encephalopathy.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill has 2 weeks of abdominal pain and distension. She has tender hepatomegaly and ascites. Her ALT is 240 IU/L (10–50). If untreated, her liver biopsy would later show fibrosis around the central veins.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying process?
questions.e: Budd-Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction, often thrombosis, causing sinusoidal congestion, hepatocyte hypoxia and later fibrosis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Prothrombotic drug and the Budd-Chiari triad.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction.

elim: Autoimmune hepatitis; does not cause sudden congestive hepatomegaly.
Gives jaundice with ALP rise and dilated ducts.
Haemochromatosis, which is gradual.
Causes portal hypertension without a large, tender, congested liver.

steps.x: **C. Hepatic venous outflow obstruction.** Budd-Chiari = blocked hepatic vein outflow → congestion → hypoxia → fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is reviewed after a fall. He drinks 40 units a week. His bilirubin is 42 μmol/L (<17), ALT 58 IU/L (10–50) and albumin 30 g/L (35–50). The team wants the single result that best reflects his liver's current synthetic function.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test?
questions.e: INR is the best marker of synthetic function because clotting factors, especially factor VII, have short half-lives; albumin falls slowly and is affected by nutrition.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Needs a fast-responding marker of hepatic protein synthesis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: INR.

elim: Half-life about 3 weeks, and lowered by malnutrition and inflammation.
Marks hepatocyte injury, not synthesis.
Excretory function, not synthetic.
Reflects hypersplenism and portal hypertension.

steps.x: **D. INR.** Best marker of liver synthetic function = INR.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure on the ward becomes sweaty and more drowsy at 3 am. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 104/60 mmHg. She was last checked an hour ago with no change. She is on IV N-acetylcysteine.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: The failing liver cannot maintain glucose homeostasis, so hypoglycaemia is common in acute liver failure; check capillary glucose first.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Sudden sweating and drowsiness in liver failure: a quick, treatable cause first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Capillary blood glucose.

elim: Needed only after hypoglycaemia is excluded.
Not a first test at the bedside.
Does not change immediate management.
Does not exclude the quick, treatable cause.

steps.x: **A. Capillary blood glucose.** In acute liver failure, check and correct glucose regularly.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has 2 weeks of jaundice and is now confused. His INR is 2.8 and ALT 4100 IU/L (10–50). He takes no medicines and his paracetamol level is undetectable. He returned from a 3 month trip to India 5 weeks ago. Ultrasound shows a normal liver with no duct dilatation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to find the cause?
questions.e: Viral serology identifies the cause of acute liver failure, especially after travel to an area where hepatitis A and E are common.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Acute liver failure with paracetamol excluded and recent travel.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral hepatitis serology.

elim: Tests for PBC, a chronic cholestatic disease.
He has no ascites.
Adds little after a normal ultrasound.
Invasive and risky with an INR of 2.8.

steps.x: **E. Viral hepatitis serology.** Cause of acute liver failure: viral serology and paracetamol level.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman, 4 weeks after giving birth, has severe right upper quadrant pain and a rapidly swelling abdomen. She has a tender liver 6 cm below the costal margin and shifting dullness. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her ALT is 310 IU/L (10–50).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins
questions.e: Budd-Chiari syndrome is confirmed by Doppler ultrasonography showing absent or reversed hepatic vein flow.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Postpartum prothrombotic state with the triad of pain, ascites and hepatomegaly.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins.

elim: Tests for infection, not venous obstruction.
Useful if right heart failure were suspected; no raised JVP.
Invasive and not the first diagnostic test.
Images bile ducts, not hepatic veins.

steps.x: **B. Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins.** Suspected Budd-Chiari = Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic veins.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman with acute liver failure is assessed on the high dependency unit. She is somnolent but rousable to voice, markedly confused and her speech is incoherent. She has asterixis. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. Her INR is 3.4.
questions.q: Which is the most likely grade of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.e: Somnolent but rousable with marked confusion and incoherence is grade III; grading encephalopathy assesses severity in liver failure.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Drowsy but rousable, gross confusion, still with asterixis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Grade III.

elim: Normal mental state.
Mild: euphoria, poor attention, sleep reversal.
Lethargy and disorientation in time, but not somnolent and incoherent.
Coma, unresponsive to voice.

steps.x: **D. Grade III.** Somnolent but rousable + gross confusion = grade III; coma = IV.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man is jaundiced 5 days after starting a herbal weight-loss supplement. He is alert and orientated with no asterixis. His ALT is 2200 IU/L (10–50) and bilirubin 98 μmol/L (<17). The team needs to know whether he meets the definition of acute liver failure.
questions.q: Which test result will decide this?
questions.e: Acute liver failure is defined by coagulopathy (INR above 1.5) with encephalopathy in a previously normal liver; the INR is the diagnostic test.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Severe acute hepatitis; the definition hinges on synthetic failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: INR.

elim: Falls slowly and is not part of the definition.
Cholestatic marker, not part of the definition.
Not part of the definition and correlates poorly.
Enzyme induction marker only.

steps.x: **E. INR.** Acute liver failure needs INR >1.5 (plus encephalopathy): diagnose it with the INR.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman is admitted with acute liver failure of unknown cause. Her INR is 2.1 and she is mildly confused. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. U&Es, glucose, clotting and LFTs have been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging?
questions.e: Liver ultrasound (with Doppler) is part of the first-line workup: it shows liver size and texture, ascites, duct dilatation and hepatic vein patency.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: acute liver failure of unknown cause
steps.x: First-line bloods sent; first-line imaging of the liver still needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ultrasound of the liver.

elim: Does not image the liver.
Only if focal neurology or a fall; she is mildly confused only.
Second-line, not first.
Shows almost nothing about the liver.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound of the liver.** Acute liver failure first-line: LFTs, INR, U&Es, glucose and liver ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with new confusion. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her abdomen is distended and mildly tender. Her CRP is 64 mg/L (<5). There is no obvious source of infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Every cirrhotic with ascites admitted unwell needs a diagnostic tap; an ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm³ confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Cirrhosis with ascites, fever, confusion and no source: think SBP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Diagnostic ascitic tap.

elim: Not useful for SBP.
Not needed first; the tap is diagnostic.
Risky and irrelevant here.
For bleeding, not infection.

steps.x: **C. Diagnostic ascitic tap.** Suspected SBP = diagnostic paracentesis (neutrophils >250).

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with cirrhosis has recovered from his first episode of hepatic encephalopathy after an infection. He is orientated, with no asterixis. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. He is going home today and the team wants to prevent a recurrence.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate medicine to prescribe?
questions.e: Lactulose is first-line for hepatic encephalopathy and is also used as prophylaxis in the community.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Recovered encephalopathy; first-line secondary prevention.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral lactulose.

elim: Not first-line and neurotoxic long term.
Outdated and nephrotoxic/ototoxic.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with cirrhosis has had three admissions with hepatic encephalopathy in 6 months. She takes lactulose and has two or three soft stools a day. There is no GI bleeding. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg. She is now orientated.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with paracetamol-induced acute liver failure is intubated in the ICU. Her intracranial pressure monitor shows rising pressure. Her pupils are sluggish. questions.stem: A 52 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has fever and abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 106/66 mmHg. Ascitic fluid shows 480 neutrophils/mm³. Gram stain is awaited. He is allergic to amoxicillin (rash).

questions.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis needs IV antibiotics first-line: ceftriaxone, cefotaxime or ciprofloxacin; a mild rash is not a contraindication to a cephalosporin.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man took 70 paracetamol tablets 20 hours ago. He is on IV N-acetylcysteine and has received 2 litres of fluid. His pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. His arterial pH is shown (see item resources). His INR is 3.1.

o: Continue N-acetylcysteine and repeat the pH in 48 hours
Give IV sodium bicarbonate and discharge when normal
Urgent referral to a liver transplant centre

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has acute liver failure from a drug reaction. Jaundice began 10 days before she became confused. She is now grade III encephalopathic. Her prothrombin time is 62 seconds (10–14) and bilirubin 340 μmol/L (<17). Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis, abstinent for 2 years, needs large-volume paracentesis every 10 days despite maximum spironolactone and furosemide and a low-salt diet. questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with cirrhosis has 6 weeks of increasing abdominal swelling. She has shifting dullness and mild ankle oedema. Her sodium is 134 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L and creatinine 78 μmol/L (45–90). A diagnostic tap shows no infection.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman took 15 paracetamol tablets a day for 3 days for toothache. She now has nausea and right upper quadrant pain. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Her ALT is 640 IU/L (10–50) and paracetamol level 30 mg/L.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man with acute liver failure from hepatitis B has a capillary glucose of 2.4 mmol/L. He is drowsy but rousable. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 106/68 mmHg. His INR is 3.0 and he is not bleeding.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman with acute liver failure on a medical ward is now responding only to pain. Her GCS is 8. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 90/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Her INR is 4.2.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man took a large paracetamol overdose 30 hours ago. His INR has risen from 1.1 to 3.4 overnight while his albumin is unchanged at 40 g/L (35–50). The trend is shown (see item resources). A student asks why the INR changed so quickly.

visual.caption: INR climbs within hours while albumin stays normal.

questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Albumin is made only in the kidney
Bile salts are needed to absorb vitamin K
Factor VII has a short half-life
Platelets are consumed by the liver
questions.e: Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors raises the INR fast because factor VII has a half-life of a few hours; albumin's half-life is about 3 weeks.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman dies of paracetamol-induced acute liver failure. At post-mortem, the liver shows necrosis concentrated around the central veins, with sparing of hepatocytes near the portal tracts. She had been drinking heavily for a week before the overdose.

NAPQI accumulation after glutathione depletion in zone 3 hepatocytes

steps.x: Centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis; alcohol induces the enzymes and lowers glutathione.

steps.x: NAPQI accumulation after glutathione depletion in zone 3 hepatocytes.

Cholestatic pattern, not centrilobular necrosis.

steps.x: **E. NAPQI accumulation after glutathione depletion in zone 3 hepatocytes.** Paracetamol: NAPQI + depleted glutathione → centrilobular necrosis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with chronic liver failure has jaundice, easy bruising, ankle oedema and early-morning hypoglycaemia. His bilirubin is 110 μmol/L (<17), with most of it unconjugated, INR 2.0 and albumin 24 g/L (35–50).

questions.e: Liver failure loses synthetic (clotting factors, albumin), metabolic (glucose homeostasis) and excretory (bilirubin conjugation) functions.

Would not explain low albumin, jaundice or hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with cirrhosis has a large upper gastrointestinal bleed. Two days later he is confused and has a flapping tremor. His serum ammonia is 140 μmol/L (<50). A student asks why a bleed makes him confused.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with antiphospholipid syndrome develops abdominal pain, ascites and a large, tender liver. Doppler ultrasound shows no flow in the hepatic veins. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Her ALT is 380 IU/L (10–50).

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman with cirrhosis has worsening ascites and swollen ankles. Her BP is 112/70 mmHg and pulse rate 86 bpm. Her albumin is 22 g/L (35–50). Urine dipstick shows no protein and her JVP is not raised.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman took 40 paracetamol tablets 5 hours ago. She feels well. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her paracetamol level at 4 hours is above the treatment line. N-acetylcysteine is started. Her pharmacist explains why early treatment protects the liver best.
